units: rainwater does not soak into paved surfaces
fast runoff reaches the stream all at once
these surges push the river out of its bed
the banks lose their fine silt to the current
bare cropland erodes in the same way
perforated paving replaces the asphalt of parking lots
cover crops open root channels that drink the downpour
planted ditches store the runoff before returning it to the subsoil
text: Rain that lands on paved ground has nowhere to go. It sheets across the asphalt, fills the drains, and reaches the stream in one hard surge instead of seeping in slowly. The river swells, jumps its banks, and strips the fine silt from the edges as it goes. Bare cropland behaves the same way, since the soil packs down and no root holds it against a downpour. The remedy is not complicated. Give the ground back its power to drink. Planners now lay perforated paving across parking lots, so grass grows through the gaps and the water sinks between them. Farmers sow cover crops between harvests, and those roots bore channels that swallow a heavy shower. Elsewhere, shallow planted ditches catch the runoff, hold it among the reeds, and let it slide down into the ground water without haste.

units: the narrator returns to a jetty she knew as a child
she remembers damp and quiet air on her old visits
the hard wind of her recent visit nearly tore her bag away
sheets of water now came over the low wall
the lighthouse keeper describes storms closer together than before
he used to count a single big warning each season
he now counts three or four between two spring tides
the narrator finds that the place of her childhood has changed character
text: I went back out onto the harbor jetty during the storm season, and I barely knew the place. As a child I used to walk out along it in a soft damp hush that smelled of salt, with the spray hardly wetting my face. That week the wind nearly ripped my bag off my shoulder, and sheets of water were coming clean over the low wall. The lighthouse keeper told me the blows arrive far closer together now, with troughs that run much deeper. Back then, he said, you logged one big warning a season. He counts three or four between two spring tides. It is not the same stretch of coast at all, honestly. The sand has melted away beside the steps, the fishermen have shifted their traps into the shelter of the mole, and the shore I carry in my head has turned into an old map you keep out of fondness.

units: a home compost bin fits into a small space
the method breaks down into three parts
the bin must sit on living soil and out of full sun
wet waste and dry material have to be alternated
meat scraps are kept out of the mixture
the pile must be turned at regular intervals to air it
moisture like that of a wrung-out sponge is what you want
the end product is a dark crumbly material that feeds the soil
text: Composting at home takes up less room than most people would expect, and the whole job breaks into three parts. Start with the container. Set a slatted bin straight onto living soil, in the light shade of a hedge, so that worms can climb up into it on their own. Then the material. Alternate a wet layer, peelings or grass clippings, with a dry one, fallen leaves or torn brown cardboard. Keep meat scraps out. They draw rodents and stall the whole process. Upkeep comes last. Turn the pile with a fork every couple of weeks, and check that it stays as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Too wet, it reeks. Too dry, it goes dormant. After two seasons you pull out a dark, crumbly material not far from the humus of a woodland floor. Spread it around your plantings to feed the ground and hold the water there.

units: a dike broke before sunrise
a night worker was the first to raise the alarm
the residents left with very little in hand
the water reached the upper floor of the low houses
the current dropped during the second half of the following night
a layer of gray silt covered the streets once the water drew off
the rescue crews set pumps on the central square
an engineer blames the break on runoff from the hillsides
text: The dike gave way just before dawn, quietly, the way a seam lets go. A night worker watched it split open from the footbridge and sounded the siren. A thick fog was still lying over the village when people came out with a bag in one hand, leaving their kitchen lights burning behind them. The flood climbed to the upper floor of the low houses, held that mark through the following night, and slackened only toward morning. What it left as it drew off was a smooth gray silt, poured through the streets like varnish. Rescue crews set pumps on the central square, and the drone of the motors took over from the silence of the water. An engineer from the river service blames the break on the runoff coming down off the stripped hillsides, which loaded the channel far past anything it was built to carry.

units: the treeless plateau loses its heat as soon as the sun goes
the heat stored in the ground rises toward a clear sky
the air against the ground falls below the dew point
the water vapor then settles as beads on the plants
a deposit of crystals forms when the surface drops below freezing
this frozen deposit draws a white rim along the edge of the leaves
cold air gathers in the hollows of the ground
the dips therefore freeze before the slopes above them
text: On a treeless plateau the surface begins shedding heat the moment the sun drops. All through the sunlit hours the ground stores energy, and it sends that energy straight up to a cloudless sky, which hands none of it back. The thin layer of air pressed against the ground therefore chills faster than the air above it. Once that layer falls under its dew point, the vapor it carries can no longer stay invisible. It settles out in fine beads on stems and spiderwebs, and we call it dew. Should the surface drop below freezing, the deposit changes character and becomes frost, a rim of white crystals along the edge of every leaf. Cold air weighs more than warm air, so it slides down the slopes and gathers in the hollows. The dips whiten well before the ground standing above them.

units: the author holds it unreasonable to cover fertile ground with buildings
a productive soil takes thousands of years to form
a sealed surface removes that resource with no way back
built surfaces make flooding worse downstream
the author would tie any further project to the repair of a derelict site
he asks that the price of land carry its power to feed people
he wants the stripping of abandoned sites made compulsory
he holds these measures to be administrative rather than technological
text: There is no sound argument left anywhere for burying our best growing ground under buildings. A fertile layer takes thousands of years to build, one crumb of humus at a time, and a concrete slab cancels it inside the space of a single building season. The loss runs well past farming. Sealed surfaces throw the rainfall downstream, where it feeds the floods that towns end up paying for. Three measures would turn this around. Tie each further project to the repair of a site already built on and since abandoned. Write the power to feed people into what a parcel of land is worth, rather than what may be put up on it. And require that derelict ground be stripped back open, so the water can reach the subsoil again. None of this waits on some invention still to come. It waits on a decision.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the warden watches over a waterlogged marsh
she reads the height of the water off graduated staffs
she likens her work to that of a nurse
she explains that a patient and a marsh are both mended by small corrections
the man before her wanted above all to drain the site
she had the old drainage ditches filled back in
the spongy growth came back after that work
the marsh now holds the water of heavy rain
text: The warden of a marsh at the bottom of a valley spends her weeks watching ground that breathes. Graduated staffs stand in the peat, and she reads the water off them, presses the moss flat with her palm, listens for frogs. She likens the work to that of a nurse. You cure nobody by shaking them awake. You adjust a little, watch, and try again. The comparison also marks how far she stands from the man who held the post before her. He wanted the place dry, cut straight ditches, and won himself a little ground that could be plowed. She had every one of those cuts filled back in. The spongy moss came up again over the peat, the brown layer thickened, and the hollow of the valley began drinking in the downpours instead of flinging them all at once at the houses lying below it.

units: the visitor expected nothing from this exhibition about climate
she came out of it delighted
a first room throws a fine spray of water over the visitors
a wind machine there works up a storm wind
a second room shows hailstones kept in the cold
a third room carries the smell of damp woodland
the visitor finds the explanatory panels far too crowded
she recommends the visit in spite of that flaw
text: Honestly, I walked into this exhibition about climate expecting nothing at all, and I came out of it delighted. Three rooms, three ideas, and no filler anywhere. The first one soaks you. Nozzles throw a salty spray over you while a wind machine works up a gale, and you grasp at once what a battered shoreline puts up with. The second room plays the cold. Behind a pane of frosted glass lie hailstones gathered after a squall, big as walnuts, sliced open to show off the rings inside them. The third goes after your nose. You step into a rebuilt patch of woodland that smells of soaked moss, with a blower pushing the scent of wet leaf mold at you. My one complaint is the panels, wordy and cramped, which nobody reads standing up. Go anyway, and save some breath for the last room.

units: the writer writes to her cousin with news of a stream
the watercourse was shut inside a concrete pipe
a group of neighbors won its return to open air
the machines opened the pipe at the start of the cold season
willows and rushes were planted along the banks
a hard rain came before the young plants had rooted
the banks held through that rise of water
dragonflies have been seen over the reopened stream
text: Dear cousin, you asked how the stream was getting on, so here is the story of the season. It began when the group of neighbors finally won the right to bring the water back into open air, after decades shut inside a concrete pipe. The machines showed up as the cold weather set in and split the slab open the whole length of the common meadow. We planted willows and rushes along the edges, mud to our knees, and by the second week the water had found a winding line of its own. Then a hard rain fell before the roots had taken hold, and we were sure we would lose the lot. The banks held, barely nicked. Dragonflies patrol the shallows over the pebbles now, and the children come hunting larvae under the flat stones. Come and see us before the thaw, you will not know the meadow.

units: the moisture laid on the leaves comes from the air itself
the nighttime cooling of the surfaces brings on that deposit
air loaded with vapor can no longer hold it in suspension
mist forms when the condensation happens in the air rather than on a surface
a cover of cloud keeps that deposit from happening
soil rich in organic matter holds more moisture
that moisture sustains the organisms that break down dead plant matter
removing the plant cover dries out this reserve
text: What lays that wet film on the leaves before daybreak? Nothing fell out of the sky. The air simply gave back what it was holding. Losing its heat to the empty dark, the skin of every plant turns colder than the air washing over it, and the invisible vapor gathers there in beads. That is dew. And when the chill takes hold of the whole body of air rather than one surface? Then the beads hang where they are, and mist spreads across the meadow. A blanket of cloud sends the warmth back down and cancels the business entirely. Where does the water go afterward? The ground drinks it, and drinks it better the more rotted plant matter it holds. That store keeps alive the countless creatures that chew through dead leaves and hand them back to the soil. Strip the cover off, and you dry out the water first, then the quiet life leaning on it.
